papers.title: Intertwined Autophagy and Integrin Dynamics Shape Axon Growth and Regeneration
papers.summary: This paper explores how autophagy, the cell's process for recycling damaged components, interacts with integrin signaling to control axon growth and regeneration. Integrins are proteins that help neurons sense and interact with their surrounding environment, and their turnover appears to be regulated by autophagic machinery. The study likely shows that manipulating autophagy affects how well axons can regrow after injury, by controlling integrin availability at the growth cone.
papers.why: Since this PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, understanding how core autophagic machinery intersects with cytoskeletal and adhesion dynamics could offer mechanistic insight applicable to interneuron health and connectivity, even though the paper doesn't directly address spatial omics or perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Molecular switches of SQSTM1: the impact of post-translational modifications on autophagy and neurodegeneration.
papers.summary: This paper reviews SQSTM1 (p62), a key autophagy receptor protein, focusing on how chemical modifications after protein synthesis (post-translational modifications) alter its function. These modifications act as molecular switches that determine whether SQSTM1 promotes or inhibits autophagy, the cell's waste-clearing process. Since autophagy dysfunction is linked to neurodegenerative diseases, understanding these switches helps explain disease mechanisms.
papers.why: SQSTM1 is a central autophagy receptor also involved in mitophagy, so understanding its regulatory switches directly informs mechanisms of mitophagy and autophagy dysregulation in neurons relevant to this project.

papers.title: Protocatechuic Acid Protects Neural Stem Cells against Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury by Suppressing JAK2/STAT3 Signaling and Restoring Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study looks at how a natural compound called protocatechuic acid (PCA) affects neural stem cells during brain injury caused by stroke-like ischemia-reperfusion. The researchers found that PCA protects these cells by blocking a stress-signaling pathway called JAK2/STAT3 and by restoring normal mitophagy, the process cells use to clear out damaged mitochondria. The overall finding is that PCA could be a therapeutic strategy to help brain cells survive and recover after ischemic injury.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly examines mitophagy as a protective mechanism in neural cells under injury conditions, which connects to the project's core focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons.

papers.title: Hippocampal neuronal progranulin mediates estrogen‑deficiency‑induced affective vulnerability and lysosomal-autophagic dysfunction.
papers.summary: This study appears to investigate how progranulin, a protein expressed in hippocampal neurons, contributes to mood-related vulnerability triggered by estrogen deficiency. The researchers link this to disruptions in lysosomal-autophagic pathways within these neurons. The work suggests a molecular mechanism connecting hormonal changes, autophagy dysfunction, and affective (mood) outcomes.
papers.why: This connects hormonal regulation of lysosomal-autophagic dysfunction in hippocampal neurons to affective behavior, offering insight into non-mitochondrial autophagy pathways relevant to neuronal proteostasis.

papers.title: Microglial SREBP2 regulate cholesterol-related lipid metabolism and inflammatory levels following ischemic stroke via the autophagy pathway.
papers.summary: This study looks at how a protein called SREBP2, which controls cholesterol production, works in microglia (the brain's immune cells) after ischemic stroke. The researchers found that SREBP2 influences cholesterol and lipid metabolism as well as inflammation levels in these cells. They show this effect happens through the autophagy pathway, the cell's process for breaking down and recycling components.
papers.why: Although this paper centers on microglia rather than neurons, its focus on autophagy-mediated regulation of lipid metabolism and inflammation in the brain after ischemic injury offers a relevant mechanistic parallel for understanding autophagy/mitophagy pathways that could inform neuronal and interneuron-focused investigations.

papers.title: Fucoxanthin enhances AMPK/mTOR-dependent autophagic flux and attenuates ferroptosis in Alzheimer's disease models.
papers.summary: This study looks at fucoxanthin, a natural pigment from brown algae, and how it affects cellular clean-up processes in models of Alzheimer's disease. The researchers found that fucoxanthin boosts autophagic flux (the flow of cellular waste through the autophagy pathway) via the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway. It also reduces ferroptosis, a form of iron-dependent cell death, suggesting a protective effect against neurodegeneration.
papers.why: This paper connects directly to the autophagy and mitophagy signaling pathways central to the PhD project, offering mechanistic insight into how autophagic flux modulation could protect neurons in disease contexts relevant to spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic studies of neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Progerin Hinders Autophagy Flux at Its Final Stages in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome Cells, Preventing Its Own Autophagic Degradation.
papers.summary: This study looks at cells from patients with Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome, a rare premature aging disease caused by a faulty protein called progerin. The researchers found that progerin blocks autophagy, the cell's waste-clearing process, specifically at the last step where cellular debris is broken down. Because this final degradation step is blocked, progerin itself cannot be efficiently removed by autophagy, creating a harmful cycle where the toxic protein builds up further.
papers.why: Since mitophagy and autophagy in neurons are central to this PhD project, understanding how a toxic protein like progerin can specifically stall the terminal, lysosomal stage of autophagic flux offers a valuable mechanistic parallel for studying autophagy blockage in the aging or diseased brain.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation-Associated Cardiac Alterations: Roles of the Kynurenine Pathway, Autophagy, and Apoptotic Signaling
papers.summary: This study investigates how neuroinflammation affects the heart, focusing on the kynurenine pathway, a route of tryptophan metabolism linked to inflammation and neurodegeneration. It also examines autophagy and apoptotic signaling as mechanisms connecting brain inflammation to cardiac tissue changes. The work highlights a brain-heart axis mediated by inflammatory and metabolic signaling.
papers.why: While centered on cardiac tissue rather than neurons, the paper's focus on autophagy and kynurenine pathway metabolism in neuroinflammation offers conceptual and methodological parallels relevant to autophagy/mitophagy research in brain tissue.
